gd_01: The guardrails. This film is different from the others — it is not about winning a deal, it is about not blowing up the company. one three seven's whole legal foundation is a single discipline: we organize and reflect the record, we never conclude. Cross that line on a call and you create real exposure, for the firm and for us. So learn these cold.
gd_02: The one rule everything hangs from: we organize and reflect, the attorney concludes. We can show what is present, what is missing, and where it came from. We can never say what the record proves, whether there is a claim, or what it is worth. Revelation is safe; conclusion is not. That single line is the moat.
gd_03: There are six bright lines. Never score or rank cases. Never state a legal deadline. Never put a dollar value on a claim. Never take a referral fee or split fees. Never guarantee an outcome. And never claim the system is flawless. We will take them one at a time — each with the wrong line, and the safe line to use instead.
gd_04: Bright line one — case scoring. Never say the system finds or ranks the strongest cases. That is the unauthorized-practice-of-law trap, and it is the single most tempting thing to say, because firms want exactly that. Say instead: we show how complete the record is against what the law requires, and your attorney decides. Coverage, not a verdict.
gd_05: Bright line two — legal deadlines. Never tell a worker or a firm that a claim must be filed by a certain date. Calculating a statute of limitations is practicing law. Say instead: the system surfaces the dates that are on the record; your attorney calculates any deadlines. We show dates — we never compute them.
gd_06: Bright line three — the value of a claim. Never say a case is worth a number, or that it is strong, or likely to settle. Say instead: we describe what is on the record — the documents, the timeline, the gaps. What it is worth is the attorney's judgment, not ours. Describe the record, not the case.
gd_07: Bright line four — referral fees and fee splitting. This one is existential. Never say we send you cases for a cut, and never price anything per case or per client. Under section six one five five and the rules of professional conduct, that is illegal fee splitting. Say instead: the worker's record is free and exportable, the worker chooses the firm, and the firm pays a flat subscription for the software. Clean money only.
gd_08: Bright line five — guarantees. Never say a worker will win, or that we improve win rates or settlement amounts. Say instead: we make the record complete and reviewable, so the attorney can decide faster. We change the quality of the file — never the outcome of the case.
gd_09: Bright line six — over-claiming accuracy. Do not oversell the A I. Never say it is flawless or never makes mistakes — that is both untrue and a liability. Say instead: we use A I to organize, and every single fact links to its source page, so anything can be verified in one click. We compete on auditability, not on being perfect. Honesty here is strength, not weakness.
gd_10: Here is the reframe that keeps you confident. These are not handcuffs — they are the moat. Every competitor that scores cases, values claims, or takes a cut has taken on legal risk and regulatory attention. Our refusal to conclude is exactly why a compliant firm can hire us. The discipline is the product. Sell it proudly.
gd_11: So when a firm pushes — and they will — do not stretch to please them. The safe move is always the same: describe the record, and let the attorney decide. If you are ever unsure whether a sentence crosses the line, it probably does. Say less, cite more, and route the hard question to counsel.
